idiom_name: ViewComponent slots: renders_one/renders_many declare where the caller's markup goes
implementation_notes: In Rails the pattern is realized by ViewComponent's slot API: the component class owns the behaviour and declares where content goes (renders_one/renders_many, documented as 'a way to render multiple blocks of content, including other components'), and the caller supplies the markup as blocks passed with with_name { ... } or as component instances and collections, while the component's own template decides placement. What replaces prop getters is the component's accessors plus the slot API: behaviour stays in Ruby methods (values, ids, ARIA state) and the caller's block renders it. Where a component would be overkill, the same inversion is written by hand as a helper that computes the state plus a partial that renders it, with content_for/yield as the layout-level form.
code_sketch:
class DisclosureComponent < ViewComponent::Base
  renders_one :trigger                       # the caller supplies this markup
  def initialize(expanded: false); @expanded = expanded; end
  def aria_expanded = @expanded.to_s          # behaviour/state stays in Ruby
  def toggle_path = @expanded ? collapse_path : expand_path
end
# caller: <%= render DisclosureComponent.new(expanded: @open) do |c| %>
#   <% c.with_trigger { button_tag("Details", aria: { expanded: c.aria_expanded }) } %><% end %>
pitfalls: Declared slots render where the component's template says, not where the caller wrote them: a slot that is never rendered disappears silently.
Slot content is captured independently of the component's later state changes, so behaviour must be exposed through accessors rather than assumed to be current.
Server-rendered components have no reactivity: each interaction needs a request cycle (or a Stimulus/Hotwire layer), so local-state assumptions do not port from client-side primitives.
Overriding a component's template while the caller also supplies slots leaves markup in two places - document which side owns what.
